chapters.name: broadcast
chapters.title: STREAMED ON TWITCH
chapters.source: Actual broadcast · earlier in this session
chapters.narration: This is RuleShift Live on my Twitch channel, streamed from a browser. Now, the connected game in close-up.

chapters.name: overview
chapters.title: CHAT BECOMES GAMEPLAY
chapters.narration: On Twitch, chat usually reacts to the game. RuleShift Live lets chat change it. Viewers propose a rule, the streamer approves it, and the rule changes actual game physics.

chapters.name: twitch
chapters.title: A REAL TWITCH PROPOSAL
chapters.narration: This real Twitch message became a proposal: every third coin reverses gravity for four seconds. The streamer has already approved it, and the viewer keeps the credit.

chapters.name: approval
chapters.title: THE STREAMER DECIDES
chapters.narration: Chat cannot activate a rule by itself. This proposal was approved before recording. I review its exact trigger and effect, then start the round. One approved rule controls this arena.

chapters.name: gravity
chapters.title: THIRD COIN. REAL GRAVITY.
chapters.narration: On the third coin, acceleration reverses and the player rises toward the ceiling. Four seconds later, gravity returns automatically. Movement and collisions follow the rule.

chapters.name: play
chapters.title: SURVIVE THE SHIFT
chapters.narration: I keep playing with the same keyboard controls. Another third-coin trigger refreshes the effect, while the arena and its solid platforms stay playable.

chapters.name: deadline
chapters.title: THE ROUND ENDS AUTOMATICALLY
chapters.source: Later in the same real round · normal speed
chapters.narration: At the end of the seventy-five-second round, the server closes the result. Effects clear, movement stops, and the final score is delivered.

chapters.name: result
chapters.title: SAVED AND TRACEABLE
chapters.narration: The result is confirmed in PostgreSQL. I can download a round record with the rule, its author, the originating message, and observed gameplay events.

chapters.name: guardrails
chapters.title: ONLY SUPPORTED RULES CAN RUN
chapters.narration: Unsupported requests cannot be approved. Chat is never executed as code. Supported proposals pass through a bounded queue, and the streamer keeps control over every activation.

chapters.name: codex
chapters.title: BUILT AND VERIFIED WITH CODEX
chapters.narration: I used Codex to build the Go application boundaries, Twitch integration, and TypeScript game engine. Here, Codex reviews the real rule and expiry logic and runs the checks. Tests cover race safety, PostgreSQL persistence, transport failures, and the game behavior.

chapters.name: source
chapters.title: ACTUAL PROJECT SOURCE
chapters.source: Read-only source and actual check results
chapters.narration: The implementation keeps domain rules independent from Twitch and storage. RuleShift Live turns audience suggestions into reversible gameplay changes, with streamer approval and an automatic return to normal gravity.

limits: Footage is automated browser testing with natural cursor paths, not a claim of a human operator.
Narration script is separate; no voice performance is synthesized or embedded.
The 8-second actual public Twitch broadcast shows the app idle; the gameplay close-ups are a separate verified Twitch-source round, not claimed to have been observed in that broadcast.
